Add Accessibility Custom Rotors Support (#269)

* Add Accessibility Custom Rotors Support

This PR adds support for capturing and displaying accessibility custom rotors in snapshots.

## What's New

**Custom Rotors**
- Snapshots now capture custom accessibility rotors configured on elements
- The legend shows rotor names, result counts, and descriptions of rotor items
- Works with both system rotors (Links, Headings, Images, etc.) and custom ones
- Shows the first several items with a count indicator if there are more
- Handles edge cases like loops and duplicate results

**Localization**
- System rotor names are now localized in English, German, and Russian
- Added localization keys for all the standard rotor types (Links, Headings, Bold Text, etc.)
- Uses the existing .lproj files pattern

**Configuration Changes**
- Changed the default for includesCustomRotors from .never to .whenOverridden
- This means rotors will show up in snapshots by default when they're defined
- You can still explicitly disable with .never or always show with .always

**Package Fixes**
- Fixed some transitive dependency issues with ObjC modules that were causing linker errors
- Added explicit dependencies on AccessibilitySnapshotParser-ObjC where needed

## Testing

Added example view with custom rotors, snapshot tests for both modes, and unit tests for the rotor parsing logic.

## Breaking Change

If you're relying on rotors being hidden by default, you'll need to pass includesCustomRotors: .never in your configuration.

Fix parser missing search fields behind zero-frame SwiftUI wrapper views (#328)

* Fix parser missing search fields behind zero-frame SwiftUI wrapper views

On iOS 26+, UIKit renders .searchable() search bars through SwiftUI
bridging views inside _UIFloatingBarContainerView. The view hierarchy
includes a _UIInheritedView with frame {0,0,0,0} that wraps the
actual UISearchBarTextField. The parser's visibility guard pruned all
zero-frame views unconditionally, so the search field was never found.

Narrow the zero-frame check: only prune when the view clips its bounds
(children genuinely invisible), is an accessibility element, or is an
explicit accessibility container (accessibilityElements != nil). Plain
wrapper views with subviews are allowed through since their children
can overflow with clipsToBounds=false.

Scope viewToElementsMap to parse call lifetime (#336)

* Scope tab bar memoization cache to parse call lifetime

viewToElementsMap was an instance property on AccessibilityHierarchyParser
that cached [UIView: [NSObject]] for tab bar context resolution. Since
TheBurglar holds a single parser instance for the app's lifetime, every
tab bar view ever parsed — and all its child NSObjects — stayed alive
forever. Over long benchmark runs this accumulated tens of GB.

Replace the instance property with a local variable passed as an inout
parameter to context(). The cache still avoids redundant tab bar parsing
within a single parse call, but the dictionary dies when the function
returns — no strong refs outlive the parse.

Don't crash the host process when the parser hits an unexpected hierarchy (#330)

* Don't crash the host process when the parser hits an unexpected hierarchy

`context(for:from:userInterfaceLayoutDirection:userInterfaceIdiom:)`
contained four crash sites that fire when the host's accessibility tree
has an unexpected shape:

* `precondition(tabBarButtons.count % tabBarItems.count == 0, ...)` —
  also crashes on `tabBarItems.count == 0` (modulo by zero) before the
  message is even reached.
* `fatalError("Can't find tab bar button in UITabBar")` when a tab bar
  button isn't in the container's tracked list.
* `accessibleElements.firstIndex(of: element)! + 1` force-unwrap on the
  `.tabBar`-trait code path.
* `assert(elementIndex != NSNotFound, ...)` when an accessibility
  container reports `NSNotFound` for one of its own elements.

The first three crash even in `-O` release builds. The parser is
increasingly used outside snapshot testing — it runs in-process against
live host hierarchies — and a host whose tree is briefly inconsistent
should not take down the host.

This change replaces all four with a `guard` that returns `nil` (no
context). The element is still parsed; it just doesn't get a series /
tab / list-bound context. Adds two regression tests covering the
container-NSNotFound and tabBar-trait-missing-button paths.

* Remove broken parser resilience test

testParserHandlesTabBarTraitViewWithUnresolvableButtons asserted
["dangling"] but the parser routes the UIAccessibilityElement child
through the .accessibilityContainer(tabBarish) branch, which produces

Fix stale safe area in tiled hierarchy snapshots (#352)

* Fix stale safe area in tiled hierarchy snapshots

Views larger than 2,000pt in either dimension are rendered in tiles,
which temporarily restructures the view hierarchy around the view.
UIKit zeroes the view's safe area when it is removed from its
superview and does not recompute it in the temporary hierarchy until
something invalidates it, so any layout driven by the safe area
(navigation bars, headers, bottom bars) shifted up by the safe area
height in the rendered image. The accessibility markers are parsed
from the restored hierarchy afterwards, so they remained correct,
producing overlays misaligned with the screenshot beneath them.

The previous compensation measured the safe area immediately after
reparenting - reading the stale zeroed value - and applied the
difference to a temporary view controller outside the view's safe
area authority chain. A view owned by its own view controller only
honors that controller's additionalSafeAreaInsets, so the
compensation had no effect for view-controller-owned views and was
unreliable even for plain views.

Instead, restore the safe area through the view controller that
actually governs the view: the view's owning view controller when it
has one, or a temporary view controller that adopts the view
otherwise. Toggling that controller's additionalSafeAreaInsets forces
UIKit to recompute the safe area, which generally resolves back to
the original value on its own; any remaining difference is
compensated through the same controller, and rendering fails with a
new ImageRenderingError case rather than silently producing shifted
content if the original value cannot be restored.

The new unit tests verify the rendered pixels: stripes positioned
relative to the top safe area inset must appear in the tiled image at
the same rows they occupy in the original hierarchy, both within the
first tile and beyond the first tile boundary. All three tests fail
against the previous implementation.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Add tall tiled snapshot test guarding safe-area alignment

The existing tiling snapshot tests are skipped because setting
usesDrawViewHierarchyInRect makes iOSSnapshotTestCase itself render
the very large annotated snapshot view blank (#75). This test only
uses .drawHierarchyInRect for the contained view's rendering - the
path that tiles - while the outer snapshot comparison keeps the
default layer rendering, which draws on the CPU and has no such size
limit.

The fixture anchors its content to the top safe area inset: a red
band fills the region above the safe area, a header sits at the
boundary, and numbered rows follow at fixed offsets, extending far
past the first 2,000pt rendering tile. If tiled rendering loses the
safe area, all content shifts up relative to the accessibility
markers and the comparison fails. Against the previous rendering
implementation this test fails with the content shifted up by the
window-propagated portion of the safe area; with the current
implementation the markers align with the content exactly.

Reference image recorded on iPhone 15 Pro (iOS 17.5).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Remove residual safe-area delta compensation

Toggling the governing view controller's additional safe area insets
already forces UIKit to recompute the stale safe area, and the
recomputed value resolves to the original in every tested environment,
so the follow-up delta compensation never fires.

The compensation also cannot stand on its own: a delta computed before
the recomputation reads the stale value, and the compensating write
itself invalidates the cache, recomputing the genuine base underneath
the applied delta and double-counting the window-propagated insets
(the regression tests fail with exactly doubled insets in that
configuration).

If recomputation ever fails to restore the original value, rendering
still fails loudly with containedViewSafeAreaCouldNotBePreserved
rather than producing misaligned output.
